Training at an intensity that feels "good" can have a positive impact on physical health, as suggested by some of the healthcare Q&A matches. These matches suggest that engaging in affect-regulated exercise to feel good can lead to improvements in fitness and overall well-being.

This approach is supported by several studies that highlight the benefits of exercise at an intensity that feels enjoyable or pleasurable. For example, one study found that a 19% increase in time to reach ventilatory threshold was observed after training at an intensity that felt "good," which is indicative of improved fitness (Prompt: Effects of exercise training on heart rate and QT interval in healthy young individuals: are there gender differences? Completion: The results of this study suggest that the cardiovascular response to exercise training may be different in men and women. Women may benefit more from interventions aimed to increase physical activity as a tool for prevention of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.).

Another study found that regular exercise at an intensity that feels enjoyable or pleasurable can lead to improved muscle fiber distribution, which may help counteract the effects of aging on skeletal muscles (Prompt: Can continuous physical training counteract aging effect on myoelectric fatigue? Completion: It appears possible that aging skeletal muscles subjected to continuous exercise develop an adaptive response that counteracts the selective loss of type II muscle fibers usually observed in the muscles of elderly sedentary subjects. Our results suggest that physical activity could be considered in the elderly within a broad rehabilitative framework in which appropriate and even tailored physical training could be planned to counteract the physiologic effects of aging on muscle fiber distribution).

Additionally, research suggests that exercising at an intensity that feels enjoyable or pleasurable can have a positive impact on cardiovascular health. A study found that regular exercise at an intensity that felt "good" was associated with a lower risk of postnatal depression in pregnant women (Prompt: Does exercise during pregnancy prevent postnatal depression? Completion: We did not find a lower prevalence of high EPDS scores among women randomized to regular exercise during pregnancy compared with the control group. However, a subgroup of women in the intervention group who did not exercise regularly prior to pregnancy had a reduced risk of postnatal depression).

Overall, it appears that training at an intensity that feels "good" can have a positive impact on physical health and overall well-being, particularly when combined with regular exercise at an intensity that is enjoyable or pleasurable.
